text: Statements: All pens are pencils. All pencils are erasers. Conclusions: I. All pens are erasers. II. All erasers are pens.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: every pen is a pencil and every pencil is an eraser, so every pen is an eraser. II reverses the chain — the erasers include the pencils, which may include things that are not pens. Only I follows.

text: Statements: Some books are red. All red things are bright. Conclusions: I. Some books are bright. II. All books are bright.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: the books that are red are bright, and 'some' is all that is claimed. II goes further than the statements allow — nothing is said about the books that are not red. Only I follows.

text: Statements: No cat is a dog. All dogs are pets. Conclusions: I. No cat is a pet. II. Some pets are not cats.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I does not follow: cats are excluded from dogs, not from pets, and a cat may perfectly well be a pet. II does: the dogs are pets and no dog is a cat, so at least those pets are not cats. Only II follows.

text: Statements: All engineers are graduates. Some graduates are employed. Conclusions: I. Some engineers are employed. II. Some employed people are graduates.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I does not follow: the employed graduates need not be the engineer ones. II does: it is just the second statement read the other way round, and 'some A are B' always gives 'some B are A'. Only II follows.

text: Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly. Conclusions: I. Some roses fade quickly. II. All flowers are roses.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I does not follow: the flowers that fade may all be flowers other than roses. II does not either — roses are among the flowers, not the whole of them. Neither follows, which is the honest answer however likely the first one sounds.

text: Statements: All squares are rectangles. All rectangles are quadrilaterals. Conclusions: I. All squares are quadrilaterals. II. Some quadrilaterals are squares.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows by the chain. II follows from I: if every square is a quadrilateral then at least those quadrilaterals are squares. Both follow — and the second is the kind of conclusion people reject for sounding too weak to be worth stating.

text: Statements: Only adults may vote. Ravi is an adult. Conclusions: I. Ravi may vote. II. Anyone who may vote is an adult.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: 'Only adults may vote' says every voter is an adult — it does not say every adult may vote, so I does not follow (Ravi may be disqualified for some other reason). II is exactly what the first statement says. Only II follows.

text: Statements: No student is lazy. Some lazy people are rich. Conclusions: I. Some rich people are not students. II. No rich person is a student.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: some rich people are lazy, and no lazy person is a student, so those rich people are not students. II claims that of EVERY rich person, which the statements never support. Only I follows.

text: Statements: All metals conduct electricity. Copper conducts electricity. Conclusions: I. Copper is a metal. II. Some conductors of electricity are metals.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I does not follow, and this is the commonest error in logic: 'all metals conduct' does not make every conductor a metal. II follows, because the metals are conductors. Only II follows — copper happens to be a metal, but not because of these statements.

text: Statements: All laptops in the lab run Linux. Some machines running Linux are offline. Conclusions: I. Some laptops in the lab are offline. II. All machines running Linux are laptops in the lab.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I does not follow: the offline Linux machines may all be elsewhere. II does not either — the lab's laptops are among the Linux machines, not the whole of them. Neither follows.

text: Statement: The college has made attendance of at least 75% a condition for sitting the semester examination. Conclusions: I. A student with 70% attendance cannot sit the examination. II. Every student with 80% attendance will pass.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: 70% is below the stated condition. II does not — attendance is a condition for SITTING the examination, and the statement says nothing about passing it. Only I follows.

text: Statement: The library will stay open until midnight during the examination fortnight. Conclusions: I. The library closes earlier at other times of year. II. Students study in the library at night.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: naming a period for later closing implies the usual hours are shorter, or the announcement says nothing. II is a reasonable guess about behaviour and not a consequence of the statement. Only I follows.

text: Statement: Of the 180 students who sat the mock test, 36 cleared every section. Conclusions: I. Exactly 20% of those who sat cleared every section. II. The test was too hard.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows arithmetically: 36/180 = 20%. II is a judgement that needs a standard to compare against — a 20% clear rate may be the intended difficulty of a screening test. Only I follows.

text: Statement: The placement cell will shortlist only students whose readiness score is in the top two tiers. Conclusions: I. A student in the third tier will not be shortlisted by the placement cell. II. Every student in the top tier will be placed.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: 'only the top two' excludes the third. II does not — being shortlisted is not being placed, and the statement describes a filter, not an outcome. Only I follows.

text: Statement: Submissions in an assessment are judged in an isolated sandbox with a fixed time limit per test. Conclusions: I. A solution that is correct but slow may still fail a test. II. No incorrect solution ever passes a test.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: a per-test time limit can be exceeded by a correct but slow program. II does not — a time limit says nothing about whether a wrong answer might match the expected output on some particular test. Only I follows.

text: Statement: Every student who reported a problem as defective had already attempted it. Conclusions: I. No student who has not attempted a problem has reported one. II. Some students who attempted a problem did not report it.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: every reporter had attempted, so nobody who has not attempted is among the reporters. (Stated as 'has reported' rather than 'can report' on purpose: the statement is about what happened, not about what the software permits.) II does not, because the statement allows for every attempter having reported, however unlikely that is. Only I follows.

text: Statement: The hostel mess will serve dinner between 7 and 9 p.m. only. Conclusions: I. A student arriving at 9.30 p.m. will not be served dinner at the mess. II. Dinner is the only meal the mess serves.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: 'between 7 and 9 only' excludes 9.30. II does not — the statement fixes the hours for dinner and says nothing about other meals. Only I follows.

text: Statement: After the new rule, no result is released until two staff members have signed it off. Conclusions: I. A result released under the new rule has at least two sign-offs. II. Results were released without any sign-off before the rule.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows directly. II does not: the rule may have raised the requirement from one sign-off to two, which is a change without the earlier state being 'none'. Only I follows — the trap is reading a new requirement as evidence of its total absence before.

text: Statement: The department will run two practice contests before any interactive problem appears in a graded assessment. Conclusions: I. No interactive problem will appear in a graded assessment before those two contests. II. The two contests will include interactive problems.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows directly. II does not, and the temptation to accept it is the point: contests carrying interactive problems are the obvious purpose of such a rule, but the statement names a condition and not its contents. The sensible purpose of a rule is not entailed by the rule. Only I follows.

text: Statement: Attendance at the mock interview is voluntary, and students who attend receive written feedback. Conclusions: I. A student who does not attend receives no written feedback from the mock interview. II. Students who attend perform better at real interviews.
options: Only I follows|Only II follows|Both follow|Neither follows
explanation: I follows: the feedback is tied to attending, and there is no mock interview to write up for somebody who was not there. II is a claim about effect that the statement does not make and could not establish. Only I follows.
